summary: Defines a generalized method of fragmentation for PWE3 protocols and services, so large pseudowire payloads can be split and rebuilt. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: If a package is too large for the truck, split it into smaller boxes and rebuild it at the other end.

questions: what are the b and e bits in pseudowire fragmentation
what is the l2tp mrru avp
when should pseudowire fragmentation be used
subtitle: A shared way to split an oversized pseudowire payload into fragments and rebuild it, for MPLS and L2TP pseudowires.

tldr.problem: A pseudowire payload plus its PWE3 and network headers can exceed the path MTU of the packet switched network.
tldr.mechanism: Two flag bits, B and E, mark the first, last and middle fragments, and the existing pseudowire sequence number orders them. The RFC says where the bits live for MPLS, L2TPv3 and L2TPv2, and adds two L2TP attributes to advertise receive sizes.
tldr.outcome: Large frames can cross the network and be reassembled at the far provider edge, though the RFC says to use this only when MTU management fails.

facts.label: MPLS B and E bits
facts.value: Positions 8 and 9 of the control word

facts.label: L2TPv3 B and E bits
facts.value: Bits 2 and 3 of the Default L2-Specific Sublayer

facts.label: L2TPv2 B and E bits
facts.value: Bits 8 and 9 of the message header

today: RFC 4623 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Fragment a Pseudowire
sections.content:
A pseudowire (PW) carries a customer's native service, such as a link between two customer edge (CE) devices, across a packet switched network (PSN) between two provider edge (PE) routers. A PW payload is normally sent as a single IP or MPLS PDU. Sometimes the payload plus the PWE3 and PSN headers is bigger than the path MTU.

This RFC defines one generalized fragmentation method for all PWE3 protocols and services. Fragmentation happens in the transmitting PE right before PW encapsulation, and reassembly happens in the receiving PE right after decapsulation. The RFC calls the span between them the fragmentation domain.

The method should be used only where MTU-management methods fail. Because of the extra processing, fragmentation and reassembly in core devices should be avoided whenever possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes a message is too big for the pipe it has to go through. Cutting it into pieces lets it pass, but it is slower, so you only do it when you have to.

sections.title: Alternatives to PW Fragmentation
sections.content:
The RFC prefers to avoid the problem. Good options are proper MTU configuration between the CE and PE and across the PSN, and adaptive measures with the originating host such as path MTU discovery (and RFC 1981 for IPv6) to shrink packets at the source.

In some cases a PE can fragment an IPv4 packet before it enters the PW, much as an IPv4 router would for packets with the DF bit clear. The fragments then go over the PW as ordinary frames, so this is transparent to the PW encapsulation and the far end, and the destination host reassembles them. IPv6 packets are not to be fragmented this way.

For L2TP over IP, the RFC says IP PSN fragmentation may be enough when the traffic needing it is light. With many fragmented PW packets, a PW-specific method can be friendlier to resources because buffers can be assigned per PW and PW sequencing can help. Deployments SHOULD avoid mixing IP PSN and PW fragmentation on the same node, and when PW fragmentation is enabled the DF bit MUST be set on all L2TP over IP packets for that PW.
sections.plainLanguage: The best fix is to make the pipe big enough or to send smaller messages in the first place. Cutting things up is the backup plan.

sections.title: The B and E Bits and Sequence Numbers
sections.content:
Fragments are marked with two bits: B (beginning) and E (ending). 00 means the whole payload is in one packet, 01 is the first fragment, 10 is the last fragment and 11 is an intermediate fragment.

Using the Sequence Number field on fragmented packets is REQUIRED. The sender first fragments the frame and then gives the fragments sequential sequence numbers. If zero is not part of the sequence space for the encapsulation, it is skipped and the number wraps from 65535 to 1.

The values are inverted relative to the Multi-Link PPP method in RFC 1990, where a complete frame has both bits set to 1. In the PWE3 version a complete frame has both at 0, so implementations that only handle complete frames can leave the bits at 0. The RFC also reuses the sequence number already in the PWE3 header instead of defining a new fragmentation header.
sections.plainLanguage: Each piece gets a sticker. One sticker says "first piece", another says "last piece", another says "somewhere in the middle", and a whole unbroken package gets none. Numbers on the pieces keep them in order.

sections.title: Signaling Support
sections.content:
For MPLS pseudowires set up with the signaling in RFC 4447, the Pseudowire Interface Parameter Sub-TLV type 0x09 (length 4), the fragmentation indicator, says the receiver can reassemble when the control word is in use. It does not oblige the sender to fragment. The sender MUST NOT fragment if the parameter is absent. Without that signaling, use of fragmentation MUST be configured in the sender.

For L2TP, the RFC defines two new AVPs, which may appear in ICRQ, ICRP, ICCN, OCRQ, OCRP, OCCN or SLI messages. The latest value received wins, and an SLI message can change it during the session.

  • MRU (attribute 94) is the largest fragmented or complete PW frame the advertiser can receive, including L2TP encapsulation but not the IP or UDP header. It alone does not imply reassembly support.
  • MRRU (attribute 95) is the largest reassembled frame, including PW framing but not the L2TP encapsulation or L2-specific sublayer. Its presence signals that the sender can receive fragments and reassemble them. A peer MUST NOT send fragments to a side that has not sent this AVP, and if MRRU is present the MRU AVP MUST be present too.

Reassembly support MAY be one-directional. Both AVPs may be hidden, their mandatory bit SHOULD be 0, their length before hiding is 8 and the vendor ID is 0. The MRRU SHOULD be used to size the reassembly buffer. For MPLS, the signaled Interface MTU SHOULD be used for the same purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: Before cutting anything up, each side says "I can put pieces back together, and my biggest box is this size." Nobody sends pieces to a friend who has not said so.

sections.title: Where the Bits Go in Each Encapsulation
sections.content:
In the preferred MPLS PW control word, the B and E bits sit at bit positions 8 and 9, followed by a 6-bit Length field and a 16-bit Sequence Number.

For L2TPv3, B and E are bits 2 and 3 of the leading bits of the Default L2-Specific Sublayer, next to the S (Sequence) bit, followed by the Sequence Number. When fragmenting, an L2-Specific Sublayer with B and E defined MUST be present in all data packets of the session, advertised through the L2-Specific Sublayer AVP (type 69) from RFC 3931. PW types with a variant sublayer are out of scope.

For L2TPv2, B and E are bits 8 and 9 of the leading bits of the L2TPv2 message header from RFC 2661. The IANA section records the new bit assignments and the AVP numbers 94 and 95, and notes the Fragmentation Indicator parameter was already allocated.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of tunnel has a little label area at the front. The RFC just says which two spots in that label hold the first-piece and last-piece stickers.

sections.title: Lost and Out-of-Order Fragments
sections.content:
Unlike Multi-Link PPP, PWE3 does not require reordering fragments. A receiver MAY drop the partly built packet when the sequence numbers show a skipped fragment, or it MAY wait for the late fragment. If it waits, a reassembly timer MUST be used so buffers are not tied up for too long.

Dropping out-of-order fragments helps scalability, but if fragments are consistently reordered, for example a short fragment always switched ahead of a longer one, the frame would never be delivered. So an implementation that fragments MUST at least send all fragments in order from its own egress point.

An implementation may also limit how many fragmented frames it reassembles per PW or across PWs. That spreads resources more evenly but can also starve frames if fragments of many frames keep arriving before any is complete.
sections.plainLanguage: If a piece goes missing, the receiver can throw the whole parcel away or wait a little. If it waits, it must set a timer so it does not wait forever.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says more complexity means more chances for errors, and implementers should take care not to let even the nastiest mix of fragments tie up too many resources. Beyond that it finds no notable security issues, and notes that RFC 1990, on which this is based, has been widely implemented.

Known IP fragment attacks use tiny fragments or overlapping offsets to get around access controls. PW fragmentation has no offset field, so overlap by offset is not an issue, but implementations MUST NOT let one whole fragment overwrite another in a rebuilt frame. To avoid tiny-fragment tricks, filtering and access controls should be applied to the reconstructed frame rather than to PW fragments.
sections.plainLanguage: Check the finished parcel, not the loose pieces, and never let a piece squash another one.
